LESSON 97 OF 106·Defensive Operations: Detect, Respond, Recover

Threat Intelligence: IOCs, TTPs and KEV

What a piece of threat intelligence can and cannot tell you, why indicators expire and techniques do not, and how a known exploited vulnerability changes what you do on Monday morning.

Applied Foundation15 min
Why this matters

Threat intelligence is only useful when it changes a decision. Indicators tell you what to look for now; techniques tell you what to build; the exploited catalogue tells you what to patch first.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • An indicator is a specific artefact: an address, a domain, a file hash. It is precise and expires quickly.
  • A technique is behaviour: how the adversary achieves something. It is durable and useful for design.
  • The known exploited vulnerabilities catalogue is a small, high-confidence list of weaknesses being used in the wild.
  • Intelligence has to be mapped to your estate, or it is just someone else incident report.
  • A feed you do not act on adds cost and false confidence, which is worse than having no feed.

The background

  • Intelligence started as a commercial feed industry selling indicator lists that were frequently stale.
  • Realised value came from understanding the adversary behind the indicators, not the indicators themselves.
  • Frameworks such as ATT&CK gave the durable layer that survives the indicator churn.
  • Government catalogues of actively exploited vulnerabilities have made prioritisation concrete for everyone.

Real-world examples

  • A blocklist updated weekly stops campaigns that started years ago and does nothing about current ones.
  • An exploited catalogue entry for a library buried in a build turns a general patch problem into a specific task.
  • Intelligence shared in a machine-readable format is usable; intelligence in a PDF is an article.

What to look for

  • Check whether consumed intelligence has led to a specific change, and find the last one.
  • Check whether your exploited-catalogue monitoring covers the products you actually run, including libraries.
  • Check whether your estate data is current enough to make an indicator useful at all.
  • Check how you evaluate a source, since an unrated feed is an unverified claim.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog

Working through the catalogue's own stated purpose and format, and applying it as a prioritisation input against a real patch queue in an environment you control

Open CISA resource ↗

MITRE ATT&CK — Software and Groups

Reading how specific tools and named actors are catalogued separately from the techniques they use, and using that separation to judge when indicator-driven and behaviour-driven defences are appropriate

Open MITRE resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Prioritise the actively exploited catalogue above severity scores, since it reflects real attacker behaviour.
  • Consume intelligence in a machine-readable format and feed it into detection and blocking automatically.
  • Map adversary techniques to your detections, which is the part of intelligence that keeps its value.
  • Score sources and drop the ones that never produce a useful indicator.
  • Review what changed because of intelligence each quarter, and stop consuming anything that changes nothing.
